body:
All pending transactions are visible in the public mempool before being confirmed. This lets bots see a profitable transaction (like a large DEX trade) and insert their own transaction with higher gas to execute first -- called front-running, a form of MEV (Maximal Extractable Value).

Common defenses:
- Commit-reveal schemes (submit a hash first, reveal the actual value later)
- Slippage limits on DEX trades (rejects execution if price moved too much)
- Using private mempools / MEV-protected RPCs (like Flashbots Protect)

WHY IT MATTERS: MEV is a multi-billion-dollar phenomenon on Ethereum. If you're building anything involving trades, auctions, or ordering-sensitive logic, front-running resistance needs to be a design consideration from day one, not an afterthought.

FURTHER READING:
- Flashbots, What is MEV: https://docs.flashbots.net/new-to-mev
- Ethereum.org, MEV: https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/mev/
homework: Take the commit-reveal example from this lesson and write the full commit() and reveal() functions with proper require() checks.

topic: DeFi building blocks: AMMs and liquidity pools
body:
Automated Market Makers (AMMs) like Uniswap let users trade tokens against a pool of liquidity instead of matching buyers/sellers directly. Prices are set algorithmically -- most commonly via the constant product formula: x * y = k.

Core idea: a pool holds reserves of Token A and Token B. When you swap A for B, you add A to the pool and remove B, keeping the product of reserves roughly constant -- which is what causes 'slippage' on large trades.

Simplified swap math:
amountOut = (reserveB * amountIn) / (reserveA + amountIn);

WHY IT MATTERS: AMMs replaced traditional order books as DeFi's dominant trading mechanism because they need no counterparty matching -- just liquidity providers earning fees. Understanding x*y=k is the foundation for understanding most of DeFi trading.

FURTHER READING:
- Uniswap V2 whitepaper: https://uniswap.org/whitepaper.pdf
- Ethereum.org, AMMs: https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/smart-contracts/#defi-decentralized-finance
homework: Given reserveA = 1000 and reserveB = 500, calculate by hand how much of token B you'd get for swapping in 100 of token A using x*y=k.

topic: Security audits: what auditors actually look for
body:
Audits systematically check contracts against known vulnerability classes: reentrancy, access control gaps, integer issues, oracle manipulation, front-running exposure, unchecked external calls, and logic errors in economic incentives.

A typical process: automated static analysis (tools like Slither) -> manual line-by-line review -> economic/game-theory review -> report with severity-ranked findings -> fixes -> re-review.

EXAMPLE of what gets flagged:
function withdraw(uint256 amt) external {
    (bool ok,) = msg.sender.call{value: amt}(""); // flagged: unchecked external call before state update
    balances[msg.sender] -= amt;
}

WHY IT MATTERS: An audit is not a guarantee of safety -- it's a best-effort review at one point in time. Many exploited protocols WERE audited. Treat audits as risk reduction, not proof of security, and combine them with bug bounties and gradual rollouts (e.g. deposit caps).

FURTHER READING:
- Trail of Bits, Building Secure Contracts: https://github.com/crytic/building-secure-contracts
- Slither static analyzer: https://github.com/crytic/slither
homework: Pick any contract you've written in this series and do a 10-minute self-audit: list 3 things an auditor might flag.

body:
tx.origin is the address that originally started the transaction chain. msg.sender is whoever called the CURRENT function -- which could be a person, or another contract calling on their behalf. They're often the same, but not always, and confusing the two is a real vulnerability.

EXAMPLE (vulnerable):
function withdraw() external {
    require(tx.origin == owner, "Not owner"); // DANGEROUS
    payable(owner).call{value: address(this).balance}("");
}

If 'owner' gets tricked into calling a malicious contract, that contract can call withdraw() on your contract, and tx.origin will still equal 'owner' -- draining funds. The fix is always using msg.sender for authentication instead.

WHY IT MATTERS: This is one of the most repeated pieces of Solidity advice for a reason -- almost every serious phishing-style contract exploit traces back to tx.origin being used where msg.sender should have been.

FURTHER READING:
- Solidity docs, tx.origin: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html#tx-origin
- Ethereum.org, Security: https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/smart-contracts/security/

body:
Deployed contract bytecode is capped at 24,576 bytes (24KB) per EIP-170. Large contracts with many functions and imports can hit this limit, causing deployment to fail entirely.

Common fixes:
- Split logic into multiple contracts (facades, libraries, or a Diamond pattern for very large systems)
- Use external libraries instead of inlining every function
- Enable the Solidity optimizer, and increase optimizer 'runs' cautiously
- Remove unused imports and simplify redundant require messages (custom errors are shorter in bytecode)

EXAMPLE (checking size with Foundry):
forge build --sizes

WHY IT MATTERS: Hitting this limit mid-project is a common, frustrating surprise for developers building anything moderately complex (like a full DeFi protocol in one contract). Knowing the limit exists -- and the standard mitigation patterns -- saves a lot of late-stage refactoring pain.

FURTHER READING:
- EIP-170 spec: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-170
- Foundry docs, contract sizes: https://book.getfoundry.sh/reference/forge/forge-build
homework: If you were building a large contract that hit the 24KB limit, name two of the mitigation strategies above you'd try first, and why.

body:
Verifying a contract means publishing its source code publicly and having Etherscan confirm the deployed bytecode matches it exactly -- letting anyone read, audit, and interact with your contract's actual functions through the UI, not just a wallet of raw bytes.

EXAMPLE (Foundry verification during deploy):
forge create src/MyContract.sol:MyContract \
  --rpc-url $RPC_URL \
  --private-key $PRIVATE_KEY \
  --etherscan-api-key $ETHERSCAN_API_KEY \
  --verify

WHY IT MATTERS: An unverified contract is a major red flag to users -- nobody can confirm what it actually does versus what you claim it does. Verification is table stakes for any contract you expect strangers to trust and interact with, and it's what enables Etherscan's 'Read Contract' / 'Write Contract' tabs.

FURTHER READING:
- Etherscan, Verify Contract docs: https://docs.etherscan.io/etherscan-v2/contract-verification
- Foundry Book, Verification: https://book.getfoundry.sh/forge/deploying

topic: Layer 2s and how they affect Solidity development
body:
Layer 2 networks (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, zkSync, and others) run mostly EVM-compatible environments on top of Ethereum, letting you deploy the SAME Solidity contracts with much lower gas costs -- but with some important differences to know.

Key differences to watch for:
- block.timestamp and block.number can behave differently (e.g. reflect the L2 sequencer, not L1)
- Some precompiles or opcodes may not be fully supported on every L2
- Bridging assets between L1 and L2 introduces delay and its own trust assumptions
- Gas cost structure differs (L2 execution is cheap, but L1 data posting cost can dominate)

EXAMPLE: deploying the exact same Counter.sol contract to Arbitrum just means pointing your deploy script at a different RPC URL -- most beginner-level contracts need zero code changes.

WHY IT MATTERS: For a beginner, the practical takeaway is: your Solidity skills transfer directly to L2s, but always check network-specific docs before relying on precise timestamp/block behavior or unusual opcodes.

FURTHER READING:
- Ethereum.org, Layer 2 docs: https://ethereum.org/en/layer-2/
- Arbitrum docs, Differences from Ethereum: https://docs.arbitrum.io/
homework: Look up one specific documented difference between Arbitrum (or Optimism) and Ethereum mainnet regarding block.timestamp or block.number, and summarize it in 1-2 sentences.
